title: The first good news (Genesis 3:15)
hookLine: even in the curse, a promise that the woman's seed will crush the serpent; Catholics see Christ and Mary here

cards: A statue of Mary stands in a side chapel. She's on a globe, hands open or folded, and under her bare feet, crushed flat, there's a snake, sometimes with an apple in its mouth.
Statues like this turn up in Catholic churches and on holy cards, easy to pass without a second look. But that snake under her heel is a Bible verse turned into stone.
It comes from a dark moment in Genesis: the fruit eaten, the blame passed around, God about to speak the consequences. And tucked into the sentence on the serpent comes a promise.

teach.b: God turns first to the serpent, curses it to crawl on its belly, and then says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel."
First, the order. Before God says a word to the man or the woman about pain and sweat and dust, God promises that evil won't win. The promise comes before their sentences.
Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus read this verse as pointing to Christ, and the Catechism calls it the protoevangelium, the first announcement of the good news.
The woman's seed will crush the serpent's head, while the serpent only strikes the heel: a wound, but not a fatal one. Third, the word she. The Hebrew says he, or it, the offspring.
The Greek Old Testament says he.

teach.h: HE IN HEBREW, SHE IN THE LATIN.
teach.b: Saint Jerome's Latin Vulgate has ipsa, she, and the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin, follows it. Modern Catholic translations such as the New American Bible follow the Hebrew. Fourth, how the Church holds both.

teach.h: THE NEW ADAM AND THE NEW EVE.
teach.b: The Catechism reads the verse as pointing to Christ, the new Adam, and to Mary, the new Eve, who shares in his victory.

So the Church doesn't need to choose between he and she: the Son crushes the serpent, and his mother stands with him. That's the statue: the promise of Genesis three, carved in stone where you'd pass it.

how: Genesis 3:9–15, 20 is read at Mass on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, December 8, and some Catholic images of Mary show the serpent under her feet.

games.why: a curse, and inside it a promise: enmity, and a crushed head. the promise comes before the man and woman hear their sentences.

practice: Bring to mind something hard that's happening now, yours or someone else's, and let it be as heavy as it is.

Then look inside it, the way Genesis tucks a promise into the curse, for one small thing still good or still on its way: a friend who showed up, a door not fully closed, a morning that will come anyway.
Hold the two side by side, and if you pray, hand both to God.

wordCard.voice: Protoevangelium. Proto, first; evangelium, gospel. The name Christians give Genesis three fifteen: the first good news, spoken in the middle of the fall.

orig.note: Latin: she herself. Jerome's Vulgate reads ipsa conteret, she shall crush; the Hebrew says he, or it.

carryVoice: Your line: the promise came first. Even in the fall, the good news gets in early. Day three hundred forty, done.
